explanations.explanation: Five men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol head out to spy out the land and explore it. That's a small crew for a big job. Hold on to that number, because these same five come back into the story.

Twelve would be a whole tour group, and the text says five. The Danites send five men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol to spy out the land and explore it. Five is a small team, and a small team can slip in and out quietly.

Two is a buddy system, and I respect that. But the text says the Danites send five men of valor from their clans. Zorah and Eshtaol are where they come from, and they head out to spy out the land and explore it.

They recognize the voice of the young Levite. They don't see him first, they hear him, and that's enough. I bet it felt like hearing a familiar ringtone in a strange place. They walk over and start asking questions.

The text doesn't mention a robe. It says the spies recognize the voice of the young Levite while they're near Micah's house. Micah is the man whose house he's staying in. Sometimes you know a person before you ever see their face.

No staff in this scene. The text says they recognized the voice of the young Levite. They were near Micah's house when they heard it, so they went over to him. I think hearing someone you know in a place you don't expect would stop anybody in their tracks.

The Levite says, "Micah has done this and that for me," and that he has hired him to be his priest. That's a pretty short summary of a whole arrangement. It's the kind of answer you give when you want to move along. Now the spies know exactly who he is in that house.

Shepherd doesn't show up here. The Levite tells the spies Micah has hired him to be his priest. He says Micah has done this and that for him, and then gives the job title. That title is what the spies pick up on next.
A scribe would be busy writing things down, but that's not the job. The young Levite says Micah has hired him to be his priest. Everything the spies ask him next comes from that one word.

They say, "Please inquire of God to determine whether we will have a successful journey." They want to know before they go. I think anybody who has ever checked the weather three times before a trip understands that feeling. The Levite is the one they ask.

They aren't asking about Micah at all. The spies ask the priest to inquire of God about whether they will have a successful journey. Their mind is on the road ahead, not on the man whose house they're staying in.

Heading home isn't on their minds. The spies ask the priest to inquire of God to determine whether they will have a successful journey. They're still on their errand, and they want an answer about how it will go.

The priest tells them, "Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey." That's what the Levite says, word for word. The spies leave with that answer in their ears. Then they head off and come to Laish.

It's true, and the text says it plainly. The priest tells them, "Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey." It's one short answer to the spies' request. After that, the five men depart and come to Laish.

The five men see people living securely, like the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting. Nothing is lacking in the land, and there's no oppressive ruler. Folks like that have no idea anyone is even looking at them. That's what the spies carry home in their report.

Armed is the opposite of what the spies see. The text says the people of Laish are living securely, quiet and unsuspecting. Nobody there is expecting trouble, and that detail matters for what the spies say when they get home.
These folks aren't afraid. The spies see them living securely, quiet and unsuspecting. When people aren't afraid, they're not watching the road for visitors. That's why the spies take note of it.

It's actually false. The text says the people of Laish were far away from the Sidonians and had no alliance with anyone. They were living like the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, but they weren't tied to them. So nobody was standing behind them.

That's right. Laish was living securely, like the Sidonians, but the text says they were far away from the Sidonians and had no alliance with anyone. Being like someone and being allied with them are two different things. That detail comes up again when the city falls.

explanations.answer: Go up and take the land
explanations.explanation: They say, "Come on, let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and it is very good." Then they push: "Why would you fail to act? Do not hesitate to go there and take possession of the land!" These guys are not asking for a committee meeting. They want action.

Peace isn't what they're pushing. The spies say, "Come on, let us go up against them." They also tell their brothers, "Do not hesitate to go there and take possession of the land!" That's a very different message from a handshake.

explanations.answer: Send more spies to be sure
explanations.explanation: More spies would only slow things down, and the spies don't want that. They tell their brothers, "Why would you fail to act?" and then, "Do not hesitate to go there and take possession of the land!" They've seen it, and they want everyone moving.

The spies tell their brothers, "God has delivered it into your hand." They also call it "a place where nothing on earth is lacking." That's their report, and they sound sure of it. All of this is what they say, and the six hundred set out afterward.

It's true. The spies tell their brothers, "for God has delivered it into your hand." That's part of their report, along with "a spacious land" and an unsuspecting people. They said it with confidence.
Six hundred Danites depart from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war. Compare that to the five who went to spy. That's a big jump, and a lot of armed men heading out together.

Close, but the text says six hundred. Six hundred Danites depart from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war. Three hundred would be half of them, and every one of the six hundred counts in this story.
Twelve thousand is a stadium crowd, and the text gives a much smaller number. Six hundred Danites depart from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war. That's still plenty of men to fill a road.

The spies say, "Did you know that one of these houses has an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol?" That's the whole list. Then they add, "Now think about what you should do." The ephod is the first thing they name, and everything on that list matters to what happens next.

This list has no silver on it. The spies name an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol. They tell their brothers about those, then say, "Now think about what you should do." That's what the six hundred hear.

No swords in that house, at least not in what the spies say. They tell their brothers it has an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol. The armed men are on the Danites' side. The spies are pointing out what's inside the house.

That's not what the text says. The five men go inside and take the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol. Meanwhile the priest stands at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men. Nobody pays for anything.

That's right. The text says the five men who had gone to spy out the land went inside and took the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol. No money changes hands. The priest stands at the gate with the six hundred armed men the whole time.

They ask, "Is it better for you to be a priest for the house of one person or a priest for a tribe and family in Israel?" That's the pitch. One household on one side and a whole tribe on the other. They put it right to him as a question.

Village is a nice word, but it's not the one they use. The Danites ask whether it's better to be a priest for the house of one person or a priest for a tribe and family in Israel. They're offering a whole tribe, which is a lot bigger than a village.

They do have six hundred armed men standing there, but that's not the word. The Danites ask the priest if it's better to be a priest for one person's house or for a tribe and family in Israel. Their offer is a tribe.

The text says the priest was glad. He took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image, and went with the people. That's the same priest who asked, "What are you doing?" a moment before. By the end of the offer, he's moving.

He is glad. The text says the priest was glad and took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image, and went with the people. He asked what they were doing, but after the offer he joined them.

After they're some distance from Micah's house, the men in the houses near Micah's house mobilized and overtook the Danites. So the neighbors call up a crowd and catch up. Micah isn't alone in this, and the Danites have to turn around and face them.

The text mentions no storm. What happens is that the men in the houses near Micah's house mobilized and overtook the Danites. The Danites were some distance away by then, but the neighbors still caught up.

The priest isn't going anywhere but forward with the Danites. He was glad and went with the people. What catches up with them is the men from the houses near Micah's house, who mobilized and overtook the Danites.

explanations.answer: You took my gods and my priest
explanations.explanation: Micah says, "You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have?" Then he turns their own question back on them: "How can you say to me, 'What is the matter with you?'" I think this one hurts a little. His answer is short and plain.

explanations.answer: You still owe me for the silver
explanations.explanation: Micah never brings up silver or money here. He says, "You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away." Then he asks, "What else do I have?" His complaint is about what they carried off.

explanations.answer: Let me come along with you
explanations.explanation: Micah doesn't ask to come along. He says, "You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away." After that, the text says he turned to go back home. He and the Danites go separate ways.

The text says Micah turned to go back home because he saw that they were too strong for him. They had six hundred armed men, and he had a crowd of neighbors. He took one look at the numbers and walked home.
Speed isn't the issue. The text says Micah turned to go back home because he saw that they were too strong for him. Strong is about numbers and weapons, not how quickly anybody moves.

Pride isn't mentioned. The text says Micah saw that the Danites were too strong for him, so he turned and went back home. I think that's a long walk, since he was going home to a house with a lot missing from it.
The text says the Danites rebuilt the city and lived there. They had burned it down, and then they settled into it. That's how the tribe finally gets a place.

explanations.answer: Leave it empty and move on
explanations.explanation: They don't leave it empty. The text says the Danites rebuilt the city and lived there. They came looking for territory to occupy, and this is where they stay.
Micah's family never gets the city. After the fight on the road, Micah went back home and that was the end of it for him. The Danites rebuilt the city and lived there themselves.
The text says they named it Dan, after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel. The city was formerly named Laish. So the old name goes out and the family name goes up.
Bethel is a real place name, but it's not the one here. The text says they named the city Dan, after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel. The city had formerly been named Laish.
Hebron isn't in this passage. The Danites named the city Dan, after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel. The old name was Laish, and the new name was a family name.

explanations.answer: As long as God's house was in Shiloh
explanations.explanation: The text says, "it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh." The Danites set up Micah's graven image for themselves, and it stayed in that spot the entire stretch. That's what Judges 18 closes on.

explanations.answer: As long as Micah was still alive
explanations.explanation: Micah's life isn't how the text measures it. It says the graven image was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh. After the road, Micah turned back home and the passage doesn't follow him again.

explanations.answer: As long as the city kept its old name
explanations.explanation: The old name didn't last long. The Danites renamed the city Dan, and the graven image was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh. That's the timeline the text gives, and it has nothing to do with Laish.
